newsitem.title: GERMANY: German gold plan hangs on slim Kohl majority.
newsitem.headline: German gold plan hangs on slim Kohl majority.

text.p: Mounting criticism within the German government's majority about Bonn's plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves raised the prospect on Saturday of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's huge gamble failing in parliament.

Two deputies, one from Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and another from the allied Free Democrats (FDP), have come out against the controversial plan and others say Finance Minister Theo Waigel must seek consensus rather than a showdown.
The problem for Kohl is that his centre-right coalition commands only five votes above the absolute majority needed to change the law and dictate Bonn's terms to the Bundesbank.

Waigel appeared on Saturday to be heading full steam ahead for a showdown by reminding the Bundesbank, which jealously guards its fabled independence from political meddling, that it must obey parliament if it decides to change the law to ensure Bonn can qualify for Europe's monetary union (EMU).

"Kohl and Waigel losing their own people -- no majority for gold law?" the popular Bild daily asked in a banner headline. Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung fronted the paper with a report that one CDU deputy had announced he would vote against Kohl.

Juergen Augustinowitz, a young CDU deputy who ranks as one of the most sceptical in the overwhelmingly pro-European party, broke the ice on Friday by announcing he would not vote for the plan, which he saw as undermining the Bundesbank.
On Saturday, FDP budget expert Juergen Koppelin urged Bonn to retreat from what is shaping up to be an unprecedented clash between the government and the central bank.
"Waigel should now give up his plan. The psychological damage would be too great," he told the Bild daily.
FDP honorary chairman Otto Lambsdorff told West German Radio Waigel would have a hard time winning support among the deputies if he did not find a compromise with the Bundesbank.
And Wolfgang Schulhoff, another sceptical CDU deputy, told the Westdeutsche Zeitung EMU could not be launched with tricks.

Augustinowitz said the Bundesbank's statement on Wednesday evening bluntly rejecting Waigel's grab for gold as dangerous for the euro and an interference in the bank's independence was "clear, unequivocal and courageous."
"I think this statement by the Bundesbank will also lead many other deputies to think again about how they will vote," he told German Radio.

Asked how many CDU deputies might oppose the gold plan, he said: "I can't give an exact number but I'm sure this clear statement by the Bundesbank and the reaction in the whole financial and banking world will not be without effect on the thinking in the CDU faction."

Kohl's bid to bend the Bundesbank to his pro-EMU will is an enormous gamble because it threatens to crack the firm wall the pro-European political class has built up against widespread concern among German voters about giving up the deutschemark.

CDU officials said last week party whips were concerned that sceptical deputies like Augustinowitz or Schulhoff could get a better hearing among fellow deputies if the EMU plan looked like too much of a risk for stability-minded voters.
Germany faces a general election in late 1998, only months before the planned start of the monetary union.
The thundering rejection by the Bundesbank could weigh far more heavily with public opinion than any number of speeches and interviews by Kohl and his allies.
"Just remember what (former European Commission president) Jacques Delors said -- 'not all Germans believe in God, but all of them believe in the Bundesbank'," a diplomat remarked.
Kohl, whose results have shrunk over his 14 years in power, was formally reelected chancellor in parliament in 1994 with only one vote to spare.
He has since mustered all his 341 delegates several times to push through critical legislation.

But none of those issues were as controversial as the gold revaluation plan, which has been widely denounced by opposition politicians, business leaders and newspaper editorialists as the kind of "creative accounting" Germany accused other European Union states of doing.
